```{r}
marks <- matrix(
  c(75, 80, 60,
    40, 50, 95,
    70, 80, 65),
  nrow = 3,
  byrow = TRUE
)

colnames(marks) <- c("Math", "English", "Science")

rownames(marks) <- c("John", "Mary", "Peter")

print(marks)
``` 
# Understanding apply()

apply() is used to perform an operation on the rows or columns of a matrix or array.

Understand the syntax:

apply(X, MARGIN, FUN)

X:	The matrix or array

MARGIN:	Whether to operate on rows or columns

FUN:	The function to apply


```{r}
apply(marks, 1, mean)
```


```{r}
# Maximum marks for each subject
apply(marks, 2, max)

# Minimum marks for each subject
apply(marks, 2, min)

# Total marks for each student
apply(marks, 1, sum)

# Standard deviation for each subject
apply(marks, 2, sd)
```
# Understanding lapply()

It applies a function to every element of a list and always returns a list.

```{r}

marks <- list(
  Math = c(75, 80, 60),
  English = c(40, 50, 95),
  Science = c(70, 80, 65)
)

print(marks)

```   
Understand the syntax:

lapply(X, FUN)

X: A list or other suitable object.

FUN: The function to apply to each element.

```{r}
lapply(marks, mean)
```
lapply() always returns a list, even when the results are just individual numbers.

# Understanding sapply()

It works similarly to lapply(), but attempts to simplify the output.

```{r}
marks <- list(
   Math = c(75, 80, 60),
  English = c(40, 50, 95),
  Science = c(70, 80, 65)
) 
```


Calculate the mean

```{r}
sapply(marks, mean)
```

Notice the difference:

- lapply() returns a list.

- sapply() simplifies the result into a numeric vector.

sapply() tries to simplify the output. It does not guarantee a vector; depending on the result, it can return a matrix or list.


# Understanding vapply()

vapply() is similar to sapply(), but it is more strict.

Understand the syntax:

vapply(X, FUN, FUN.VALUE)


X: Input list
FUN:	Function to apply
FUN.VALUE:	Expected output type and size

Example: Calculate the mean

```{r}
vapply(marks, mean, numeric(1))
```

Why numeric(1)?

Because the mean function returns one numerical value for each subject.

```{r}
vapply(marks, function(x) {

  c(
    Mean = mean(x),
    Median = median(x),
    Minimum = min(x),
    Maximum = max(x),
    Variance = var(x),
    Standard_Deviation = sd(x)
  )

}, numeric(6))
```

Why numeric(6)?

Because our function returns six numerical values for each subject.
